Orchot Tzadikim 2:36: The humble man rejoices in the portion the Holy One, blessed be He, has allotted to him, whether much or little, as it is said (Psalms 37:16), "A little that a righteous man has is better [than the abundance of many wicked]." And through this his heart is at rest from the turmoil of this world, and through this his heart is free to seek out wisdom and the service of the Holy One, blessed be He.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:37: The humble man judges every person favorably. A parable: one of the pious was asked, how did you merit to become a master over the people of your generation? He answered: because every person I saw, I regarded as better than myself. If he was wiser than I, I said: he must also fear God more than I, because of his greater wisdom. And if he was lesser than I in wisdom, I said: he sins unwittingly and I sin deliberately. And if he was older than I, I said: his transgressions are fewer than mine. And if he was equal to me in wisdom and in years, I said: his heart is better toward God than mine, for I know the transgressions I have committed, but I do not know the transgressions he has committed. And if he was richer than I, I said that he gives more charity than I. And for these reasons I would honor people, and I would submit before them.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:38: The flaws of the humble man are forgotten, because people wish for his honor, and also his supporters are many. A parable: it was said of one of the kings that many men were sleeping one night, and he himself arose and adjusted the lamp so it would not go out. They said to him: why did you not command us? He said to them: I arose as king and I have returned as king.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:39: And they said: every virtue is envied, except for humility. And they said: whoever is lowly in his own eyes is great in the eyes of others.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:40: But this is what one must guard against in this trait: that one not be humble and submissive before the wicked. And of this the verse says (Proverbs 25:26), "as a muddied spring and a corrupted fountain is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked." And if he has the ability, he should take vengeance upon the wicked for the honor of the Name, and strengthen his rebuke against them, and stand against them like a roaring lion to save the robbed from the hand of the robber. And he should instruct people in the service of the Holy One, blessed be He, and rebuke them with all his strength, according to his wisdom — at first gently, and if this does not help, he should shame them. And he should command what is good and warn against what is evil, with his mouth and his tongue, according to his wisdom; and he should hasten to exact God's judgments from whoever is liable for them, and not submit or be lowered in this.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:41: There is a humility that is as bad as pride, such as the matter the false prophets did, who wore garments like the true prophets so that their lies and falsehoods would be accepted, as it is said (Zechariah 13:4), "and they shall not wear a hairy mantle in order to deceive."
Orchot Tzadikim 2:42: Therefore, those who go about humbly in the matter of dress, and speak gently, and conduct themselves in the guise of the pious and the righteous, so that people will believe them and rely on their words, and flatter those who should not be flattered, and act deceitfully in secret, and are careful to fulfill the commandments only in public and not when they are alone, and steal people's minds — these desecrate the Blessed Name more than any other person, and cause the world not to believe the truly good; and they are suspected by people, who say: perhaps these too are like those. And whoever recognizes them is obligated to publicize and make it known to all, as our Sages said (Yoma 86b): the hypocrites are publicly exposed.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:43: Therefore awaken, and do not overlook the need to weaken the haughtiness and deceit within you. And do not refrain [from correcting yourself] because you see many of your peers acting this way, not removing their haughtiness and deceit, and saying to those who rebuke them: "who is the man who has no pride? And who is the man who can be careful to be upright in business dealings, and not deceive people, and do all his deeds properly? Are there not many people better and greater than I who do such and such? Therefore I too shall do as they do, and whatever will be theirs in the World to Come will be mine as well." Those who think this way commit a folly beyond compare. A parable: whoever's eyes hurt, and there is a salve that is proven effective for healing the eye, and the truth of this remedy is already known to all — it is no wisdom to say, "I will use no remedy at all, and if I go blind, what of it? How many blind people are there in the world, and whatever will be theirs will be mine as well." Is this not mockery and folly before all?
Orchot Tzadikim 2:44: Therefore examine your own soul, and strive with all your strength, and do not fix your eyes on one who is below you in the virtue of wisdom and in the service of the Holy One, blessed be He, for by this you will fall short in service and in wisdom. Rather, fix your eyes and your heart on one who is above you, and strive to pursue him and to reach him as best you can in the virtue of wisdom and in the service of the Holy One, blessed be He. And of this it is said (Hosea 6:3), "then let us know, let us pursue the knowledge of the Lord; His going forth is sure as the morning, and He shall come to us as the rain, as the latter rain that waters the earth."
Orchot Tzadikim 3:2: Shame. Our Sages said: understanding is shame, and shame is understanding. For of Adam and Eve it is said (Genesis 2:25), "and the two of them were naked, the man and his wife, and they were not ashamed" — for they did not yet know modesty and could not distinguish between good and evil. And after they ate from the Tree of Knowledge it is said (ibid. 3:7), "and the eyes of them both were opened."
Orchot Tzadikim 3:3: And so all living creatures other than man have no shame, since they have no understanding. And every wise-hearted man knows the virtue of understanding and wisdom, for through it he attains the truth of things, and through it he attains the recognition of the unity of his Creator, blessed be He, so as to serve Him, and through it he can become like the angels.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:4: And since the virtue of wisdom is so great, its companion trait, similar to it, which is the trait of shame, must be close to it. And here is the proof: you have never seen a shame-filled person lacking in understanding, nor a knowledgeable person without shame. Therefore every person ought to strive and conduct himself with this important trait, using wisdom to acquire it until it is firmly fixed in his soul; and he should make it dominant over all his natural inclinations, and it should be more important in his eyes than his other traits, for through it he attains most virtues, and is restrained from transgressions and from all disgraceful traits. The trait of shame is a fence and an iron partition before all transgressions, for a person commits many transgressions in private that he would be ashamed to commit before people.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:5: And so our Sages said (Berachot 28b): at the time of the passing of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, his students said to him: our master, bless us! He said to them: may it be [God's] will that the fear of Heaven be upon you as the fear of flesh and blood. They said to him: only that much and no more?! He said: would that it were so! Know, that when a person commits a transgression in private, he says: no man will see me. And all this is because he fears coming to shame; and he refrains from transgressions because he would be ashamed before people, for from [performing a commandment] not for its own sake one comes to [perform it] for its own sake (Pesachim 50b).
Orchot Tzadikim 3:6: But the highest level of the trait of shame is that a person be ashamed before the Holy One, blessed be He, as the matter is stated (Ezra 9:6), "My God, I am ashamed and embarrassed to lift up my face to You, my God." And should you think: how can I be ashamed before one whom I do not see with my own eyes? — truly you must know that although the Holy One, blessed be He, is hidden from the eyes of every living being, He is found within hearts and revealed in thoughts. And a person attains the levels of shame by secluding himself to contemplate the greatness of the Blessed Lord, and by always remembering that the Holy One, blessed be He, sees his deeds, examines his innermost being, and observes his thoughts. A parable: one of the sages said: if you have been careful all your days not to sin, do not credit yourself for it, for the beginning of abandoning transgressions is generally because one is ashamed before people. Therefore a person must be very careful about this, to bear in mind, when abandoning transgressions, that he not abandon them merely out of shame before people. For the inclination draws his heart to this matter: if you do such-and-such, people will shame you. Therefore a person must make it the very first of all first principles that he know his Maker and recognize His power, and set his heart on whom he is to serve and whom he is to fear, at whose command he is to act and who has warned him — as David said to his son Solomon (1 Chronicles 28:9), "know the God of your father, and serve Him." And through this matter he will attain being ashamed before the Holy One, blessed be He, alone.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:7: It is a known and clear thing that all people do many things in private, and likewise speak many things in private and think many thoughts, and are concerned only that these matters not become known. And if all the deeds they did from their youth, and all the words they spoke, and all the thoughts they thought were revealed and known to every person, they would be ashamed with a very great shame. How much more so, then, must one be ashamed before the Holy One, blessed be He, who looks into hearts, and sees thoughts, and knows all the deeds, words, and thoughts a person has done all his days, before whom there is no forgetting — one must be ashamed and disgraced before Him.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:8: There are four levels of shame. The first: one who is ashamed to commit transgressions openly, but commits transgressions in private — this one steals the awareness of the One above, for he is ashamed before the world but not before the Blessed Lord; and his wickedness is very great.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:9: The second: one who is ashamed before the world, and also in private refrains from transgressions, because he fears it might become known to people, and he would be ashamed before them. Of this they said (Pesachim 50b): from [performing a commandment] not for its own sake one comes to [perform it] for its own sake.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:10: The third: if he thinks, "how can I do this evil thing in private, when I would be more ashamed before a servant than before a master, and steal the awareness of the One above?!" — and through this refrains from the transgression, this is a good level.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:11: The fourth: if a person is ashamed, openly and in private, before the Blessed Lord alone — there is no level higher than this level.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:12: Our Sages said (Berachot 12b): whoever commits a transgression and is ashamed of it — all his iniquities are forgiven him. And they further said (Avot 5:20): shamefacedness leads to the Garden of Eden. And our Sages said: shame and faithfulness are bound one above the other, for the shame-filled person holds fast to faithfulness with every person, and whoever is not faithful has no shame. The wise man said: when you feel no shame, you will do whatever you please.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:13: A person should accustom himself never to do anything that his fellow would be ashamed to tell him to stop. For instance, a person who has a private matter, and his fellow enters upon him and is ashamed to tell him to leave; or one who lodges in his fellow's house, and the host is troubled by it but is ashamed to tell him to leave; or one who reads his fellow's letters, and his fellow is ashamed to tell him not to read them — and all such matters.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:14: He should be very careful about this matter, not to burden himself upon anyone in any way, and not to ask anything of him as a gift — whether to borrow his utensils or his money — in a case where he knows the other does not do so willingly, yet is ashamed to turn him away empty-handed.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:15: And whoever has the trait of shame finds it hard to bear that his fellow feels shame because of him. And of this the wise man said: love no one except one who shows himself as though he cannot manage without your help, even though in truth you need his help more than he needs yours; and if you wrong him, he will forgive you, and make himself appear as though he were the one at fault; and he will ask of you things he does not need, so that you should not be ashamed to ask things of him.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:16: And whoever wishes to accustom himself to shame should always sit in the presence of one before whom he feels shame.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:17: And he should not debase the dignity of his own face by asking things of people, for once you have debased the dignity of your own face, you will find no one who can restore it to you.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:18: There is one who shames his fellow, not because he hates him, but in order to remove his own shame. For instance, he does something shameful, and says: what have I done? Did not so-and-so and so-and-so do the same as I? And by this he lightens his own shame at the other's expense. And there are great evils in this: first, that he shames others for his own benefit; second, that this makes it harder for him to repent, for he will think, what have I done? Did not so-and-so and so-and-so do the same? And third, that he causes the many to sin, for through this the sin will seem light in his eyes, since he has removed the shame from that sin.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:19: And if he says something false about others in order to lighten his own shame — then his punishment is very great, for he casts blemish upon the upright. And many more evils are bound up in this.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:20: There is one who is ashamed to refrain from transgressions. For instance, when the people of his town are accustomed to certain known transgressions, such as gazing at women and the like of other transgressions, and they shame whoever refrains from this, and mock whoever does not follow their ways — in such a case one must strengthen himself to bear the shame, and must refrain from the transgressions even if he will be shamed for his abstention.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:21: And likewise there is one who is ashamed to fulfill commandments that people are not accustomed to fulfilling. And whoever fulfills commandments that people are not accustomed to, must nonetheless bear it and fulfill those commandments; and no commandment should be abandoned because of shame, for one must be ashamed before the Creator, blessed be He, who commanded these commandments.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:22: For this is a clear matter: a king's servant will not abandon the king's command, even if he must bear great shame from the people who mock him for doing what his master commanded him. And whoever cannot bear shame in the place of a commandment, and is ashamed to perform the commandment, and abandons the good path because of shame — this shame is very bad. And likewise if he is ashamed to admit the truth — this too is a very bad affliction. And likewise if he is ashamed to rebuke people and to command them regarding the good. And likewise if he sits before his teacher and is ashamed to ask about what he does not know, whether it be a small or a great matter — this is very disgraceful. And of this the verse says (Proverbs 30:32), "if you have acted foolishly by exalting yourself, or if you have plotted evil, put your hand over your mouth." And our Sages said (Avot 2:5): the shame-filled person does not learn. Rather, the straight path is that one should not be ashamed to ask about what he does not know, whether a small or a great matter. Behold, you see David, king of Israel, who said (Psalms 119:46), "and I will speak of Your testimonies before kings, and shall not be ashamed."
Orchot Tzadikim 3:23: A pious man ("chasid") is called by the name of shame, for "chasid" is a term related to "white," for the Targum renders "and the stork (chasidah)" as "chavarta" [the white one] (Leviticus 11:19). And similarly, "nor shall his face now grow pale (yechevaru)" (Isaiah 29:22). The Targum of "disgrace (cherpah)" is "chisuda." And why all this? Because the pious man must bear shame in order to fulfill the Torah, and must set aside shame from his face in the place of a commandment; and then he is called "chasid," and through this he attains prophecy, as it is written (Psalms 89:20), "then You spoke in a vision to Your pious ones (chasidecha)." And through his shame he attains the fear of Heaven, as it is written (Exodus 20:17), "and that His fear may be upon your faces, that you sin not" — what is a fear that is recognizable upon the face? You must say: this is shame (Nedarim 20a).
Orchot Tzadikim 3:24: And he must be very careful never to shame any person, for our Sages said (Bava Metzia 59a): whoever whitens the face of his fellow in public has no share in the World to Come. Whitening a person's face is a shade of murder, for the red drains away and white comes in its place (ibid. 58b), resembling the draining of blood at death. And so our Sages further said (Berachot 43b): the anguish of being shamed is more bitter than death; therefore a person should throw himself into a fiery furnace rather than whiten his fellow's face in public. And they learned this from Tamar: even though she was being taken out to be burned, she did not wish to shame Judah publicly. And even in a place of rebuke the Torah said (Leviticus 19:17), "and you shall not bear sin because of him." How so? One should rebuke him at first privately and gently; but if you rebuke him at first in public and shame him, you thereby bear sin because of him (Arachin 16b). How much more so one who shames his fellow when it is not even a matter of rebuke.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:25: And the destruction of Jerusalem came about through the shame of the incident of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza (Gittin 55b).
Orchot Tzadikim 3:26: Therefore a person must be very careful never to do anything that would bring shame to any person in the world. Even in matters of Torah study, if he is discussing and debating with his fellow and hears that his fellow has erred, he should not say to him, "you have erred" or "you do not understand" or the like, so that he not be shamed; rather, he should act as though he did not notice that the other had erred. Likewise he should not give a nickname to his fellow, so as not to shame him; but if he wishes to speak of someone who has such a nickname, even not in his presence, he should say, "so-and-so from such-and-such a place," or "the son of so-and-so," or give identifying details, until he is recognized without using the nickname.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:27: And a person should not say, in public or privately, "so-and-so wanted to give me his daughter [in marriage], and I did not want her" — for by this he confers honor upon himself and shame upon his fellow. And likewise he should be careful in every matter that no shame come to his fellow through his words.
Orchot Tzadikim 3:28: A person should always be among those who are insulted but do not insult, who hear their own disgrace and do not answer. And of them it is said (Judges 5:31), "and they who love Him shall be as the sun going forth in its might" (Shabbat 88b) — measure for measure: since he heard his own disgrace and his face turned pale with the shame, the Holy One, blessed be He, will make his face shine brighter than the light of the sun, as the matter is stated (Isaiah 60:1), "and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you."
Orchot Tzadikim 3:29: From the trait of shame one attains humility, for one submits to people because of his shame. And one attains the trait of modesty, for the shame-filled person is ashamed to do his deeds openly. Our Sages said: in worthy children, shame is visible upon their faces, for whoever is shame-filled is a sign that he is of the seed of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Yevamot 79a). Our Sages said: shame becomes known at a time of anger. And they said: the hatred of the shame-filled person is better than the love of a fool. A person must feel shame before every person, and place upon his face the mask of shame, as you know of the matter of Saul when he hid himself, as it is said (1 Samuel 10:22), "behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage" — and God chose him for kingship, as it is said (ibid. verse 24), "do you see whom the Lord has chosen?" Our Sages said: this trait is among the finest conducts of the precious soul,
Orchot Tzadikim 3:30: and it corresponds to the perfection of the body. And whoever feels shame, his own stature grows the greater for it. And examine and reflect on this all the more.
